newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says "terrorism" blocking Iran relations.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says "terrorism" blocking Iran relations.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said Iran's support of political violence stood in the way of a thaw in relations between the two countries.

Mubarak said in a television interview broadcast late on Tuesday that he showed Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati documents to prove Tehran's role in political violence when the Iranian minister visited Cairo earlier this month.

Velayati came to Cairo to invite Mubarak to an Islamic summit in Tehran in December. Mubarak did not say if he would go or not, but Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said while Velayati was here that it was too early to say.
"I took the invitation from him (Velayati). I talked to him about terrorism issues," Mubarak said. "I told him the problem of terrorism is a main obstacle in the matter (of establishing ties)."
Mubarak has accused Iran and Sudan of backing an attempt by Egyptian militants to kill him in Addis Ababa in 1995. Both countries deny the charge.

"Most of the terrorist operations that they deny a role in are planned there (Iran). This means some people who are giants in terrorism are there till now. He denies this. But our information indicates they (terrorists) are there between Afghanistan and Iran," Mubarak said.

"They leave from there to Sudan and many other countries. He said his country's borders were 8,000 km long. I told him we should collect all the terrorists from around the world, since they cross your borders, and let them live there and leave us in peace. He laughed," Mubarak added.

Egypt, along with most Arab countries with their predominantly Sunni Moslem populations, has viewed majority Shi'a Iran with suspicion since the revolution that swept the Shah out of power in 1979 and brought in a strict theocracy.
Egypt incensed Iran by granting asylum to the Shah, who was buried in Cairo when he died, and by signing a peace treaty with Israel, also in 1979.

Tehran cut diplomatic ties with Egypt later that year and the two sides have maintained a cool distance since. Although they opened interest sections in 1991 and have since developed trade ties, full relations have not been re-established.

Egypt, locked in a low-level guerrilla war with Moslem militants, has often accused Iran of trying to export its Islamic revolution throughout the region, particularly to Egypt's southern neighbour Sudan, where an Islamist-backed military government took over in a bloodless coup in 1989.

Velayati's visit to Cairo was the first by a high-ranking Iranian official since 1994 when Velayati came to attend a Non-Aligned Movement meeting of foreign ministers and a United Nations population conference.

Mubarak said in comments published in government newspapers on Wednesday that Egypt had overcome diplomatic difficulties with Iran and sent two plane-loads of aid to help with relief efforts there earlier this week after a massive earthquake.
